name: Supplier Diversity (Min 2 Per Critical Component)
description: Maintain at least two independent trusted sources for every critical component. Eliminates single points of failure and enables cross-reference for detecting anomalies. Where market constraints limit diversity, apply compensating mitigations.

current_state.summary: Multi-vendor frontier training is demonstrated rather than hypothetical: Anthropic trains and serves Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs and NVIDIA GPUs simultaneously, with roughly 500,000 Trainium2 chips in Project Rainier and a partnership to deploy up to 2GW of AMD Instinct MI450. NVIDIA's revenue share has been falling rather than rising. It remains rare and costly - CUDA lock-in and the porting burden are the residual barriers, not the absence of alternatives.

technical_feasibility.notes: For most components (networking, storage, servers): feasible. For AI accelerators specifically: market structure makes true diversity very difficult. Training frameworks may not port cleanly between vendors.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Qualifying second source, integration testing, framework porting, operational experience. For accelerators: may need to accept generation gap between primary and secondary supplier.

cost.notes: Maintaining two parallel hardware stacks is very expensive. Different drivers, different frameworks, different debugging tools. Operational overhead is massive.

vendor_dependency.notes: Entirely depends on market offering viable alternatives. Can't create diversity where it doesn't exist.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Competitive AI accelerator alternatives at frontier scale
supply_scarcity.notes: Frontier accelerators remain allocation-constrained and lead times are long, but the market is diversifying rather than consolidating: NVIDIA's share has fallen from roughly 87% to an estimated 75%, with AMD and hyperscaler custom silicon taking the difference.

organizational_readiness.notes: Multi-vendor strategy is familiar conceptually but extremely expensive in practice for ML workloads.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without supplier diversity, a supply chain compromise of the single vendor affects ALL deployed hardware simultaneously. No behavioral cross-reference is possible — compromised hardware behaves the same as legitimate hardware because there's no baseline from an independent source.

open_questions.question: Is meaningful accelerator diversity achievable given market concentration?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Must accept single-vendor risk for accelerators and rely on compensating controls (inspection, attestation)

real_world_parallels.description: The US military requires at least two qualified suppliers for critical munitions components (DFARS requirements). When sole-source situations arise, additional inspection and testing compensates.

name: Upstream Hardware Inspection (Pre-Facility)
description: Extends the facility inspection pipeline (PHY-07) upstream: sampling and verification at vendor sites, in transit, and at receiving, before components ever reach the datacenter. Reuses PHY-07's equipment, staff and golden-reference corpus, so this block is the incremental cost of the upstream reach - chain-of-custody, vendor-site access, and the logistics of intercepting hardware early - not a second lab.

current_state.summary: No AI lab inspects hardware upstream of its own receiving dock. Government defense procurement does some of this through trusted-supplier programs, but the practice depends on contractual access to vendor facilities that commercial buyers rarely have. The capability is meaningless without a reference to compare against, which is why it is gated on provenance tracking and supplier diversity.

technical_feasibility.notes: Same as PHY-07. Individual techniques proven; scaling to volume and automating detection is the challenge.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Shorter than PHY-07 because the lab already exists; the time is spent negotiating vendor-site access and standing up chain-of-custody, not procuring equipment.

cost.notes: Incremental over PHY-07, which carries the equipment and lab cost. What is left is chain-of-custody logistics, vendor-site access (often a contractual fight rather than a purchase), and the sampling overhead of intercepting hardware before it ships. Deploying this without PHY-07 would cost far more, because the lab would have to be built first.

vendor_dependency.notes: The binding constraint. Upstream inspection requires suppliers to permit sampling at their own facilities, which defense procurement obtains contractually and commercial buyers generally cannot. Without that access the block degrades to receiving-dock inspection, which PHY-07 already covers.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Hardware inspection specialists for modern semiconductors

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Same as PHY-07 — without inspection, supply chain compromises (hardware implants) go undetected.

completed_by.why: An inspection pipeline can only flag deviation from a reference. Without provenance tracking and a second supplier to cross-reference against, there is no golden sample and a uniformly backdoored batch passes.

name: Adversarial Content Screening for Training Data
description: All external data entering the SL5 environment screened for adversarial content: poisoning attacks in training data, jailbreak attempts, adversarial examples, malicious code. Mandatory staging isolation until screening completes. Human review of flagged content.

current_state.summary: Active research problem, and 2025 results made it look structurally harder. Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found that poisoning required a near-constant number of documents regardless of model and training-data size - about 250 documents backdoored models from 600M to 13B parameters, which for the larger model is 0.00016% of training data. The study tested a narrow denial-of-service backdoor and its authors note that applicability to larger models and more harmful behaviours remains unclear. If the result does generalise, it implies screening would need recall approaching perfect over the entire corpus, since attack cost would not scale with corpus size. The SL5 Standard explicitly marks this as an open question.

technical_feasibility.notes: Fundamental research problem. Adversarial robustness remains unsolved. Best-effort detection catches unsophisticated attacks but sophisticated adversaries can bypass current detectors. The SL5 Standard acknowledges breakthroughs are needed.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Basic staging isolation: 6 months. Effective detection against sophisticated adversaries: unknown timeline, research-dependent.

cost.notes: Research investment + detection infrastructure + staging environment + human review team. The research component has uncertain ROI.

vendor_dependency.notes: Depends on broader research community progress. Can invest internally but problem may require field-wide breakthroughs.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Researchers at the frontier of adversarial robustness
supply_scarcity.notes: Very small research community. Most work is academic. Translating to operational detection is additional gap.

organizational_readiness.notes: AI labs have ML research capability. But the security research needed is different from capability research. Also: screening terabytes of training data is operationally challenging.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without adversarial content screening, an adversary can poison training data to install backdoors (model behaves normally except on adversary-chosen triggers), degrade model performance subtly, or cause the model to assist in its own exfiltration. Web-scale training data makes this especially easy — inject poisoned content into crawled web pages.

open_questions.question: Is robust adversarial content detection achievable against sophisticated adversaries?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: SL5 cannot fully protect against training data poisoning — must limit to known-good data sources (dramatically restricting training data availability)

real_world_parallels.description: Antivirus/malware detection has been an arms race for 30+ years with no complete solution. Adversarial content detection for ML is the same problem in a new domain — and the attackers have a structural advantage because detection is harder than evasion.

name: Sub-Tier Flow-Down of Security Requirements
description: Security requirements contractually flow from prime contractors to all sub-tier suppliers (2nd, 3rd, 4th tier). Due diligence on upstream dependencies ensures that a vulnerability in a sub-contractor doesn't compromise the primary supply chain.

current_state.summary: NIST SP 800-161 Rev 1 provides guidance. Some defense contractors implement flow-down. AI labs typically have no visibility beyond tier-1 suppliers. The depth of modern supply chains (hundreds of transitive dependencies) makes full flow-down extremely challenging.

technical_feasibility.notes: Contractually feasible for tier-1 and tier-2. Practical visibility into tier-3+ is very difficult. Transitive dependencies in hardware (hundreds of components from dozens of countries) make complete flow-down arguably infeasible.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Contract renegotiation + supplier assessment + audit capability + ongoing monitoring. Existing supplier relationships may resist new requirements.

cost.notes: Legal/procurement staff + supplier assessment team + audit program. Cost scales with supplier count.

vendor_dependency.notes: Requires cooperation from all major suppliers. They must agree to flow-down requirements in contracts and permit audits.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Supply chain security auditors with semiconductor industry knowledge
supply_scarcity.notes: SCRM professionals exist in defense space. Semiconductor-specific expertise rarer.

organizational_readiness.notes: Suppliers may resist requirements (especially transparency about their own sub-suppliers). Global supply chains cross jurisdictions where enforcement is limited.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without flow-down, the weakest link in the supply chain is an unvetted sub-tier supplier. A firmware contractor three levels deep may have no security requirements at all — but their compromised code runs on your servers with full privilege. See Chain 6 (Remote Ghost).

real_world_parallels.description: SolarWinds (2020): compromise of a build system at a single software vendor cascaded to 18,000+ organizations. The attack exploited exactly the sub-tier visibility gap — most victims had no relationship with or visibility into SolarWinds' build infrastructure.

name: Counterfeit Detection (QBL/QML)
description: Anti-counterfeit program using Qualified Bidders Lists (QBL) and Qualified Manufacturers Lists (QML). Only procure from pre-qualified suppliers. Detect counterfeits via electrical testing, marking verification, and provenance tracking.

current_state.summary: Government uses QBL/QML for defense procurement. Trusted Foundry program available for government contractors. AI labs procure from distributors with basic authenticity checks but no formal QBL/QML program.

technical_feasibility.notes: QBL/QML process is well-defined. Challenge for AI labs: Trusted Foundry requires government contracts (not available to private sector without government cooperation). Private equivalent must be built.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Supplier qualification process + testing infrastructure + procurement policy changes. Government cooperation accelerates if available.

cost.notes: Supplier qualification + testing + procurement team expansion. Moderate cost.

vendor_dependency.notes: Testing labs exist. Trusted Foundry access requires government relationship.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Counterfeit detection capability for advanced semiconductors
supply_scarcity.notes: Testing labs exist. Expertise for detecting sophisticated counterfeits (vs obvious fakes) is rarer.

organizational_readiness.notes: Restricting to qualified suppliers may limit procurement speed and options. Manageable with planning.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without counterfeit detection, an adversary can substitute compromised components that appear identical to legitimate ones. Counterfeit chips may have modified functionality (backdoors) or simply fail at critical moments (denial of service).

real_world_parallels.description: Counterfeit electronic parts have been found in US military systems multiple times. A 2012 Senate Armed Services Committee investigation found 1,800+ cases of counterfeit parts in DoD supply chains.

name: Component Provenance / Authenticity Tracking
description: Cryptographic attestation of component origin and chain of custody. Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), Model Cards, Datasheets with cryptographic signatures. Enables verification that each component is what it claims to be and has traveled through expected supply chain path.

current_state.summary: SBOM tooling and standards continue to mature - CISA's 2025 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials expanded the technical standard and names AI software as an area for further consideration rather than adding AI-specific elements - but the federal mandate reversed: OMB M-26-05 (January 2026) rescinded the vendor self-attestation requirement in favour of an agency-led risk-based approach. Hardware provenance is much less mature and now advances through industry consortia (Caliptra, OCP S.A.F.E., DICE, SCITT) rather than policy; hardware bill-of-materials templates remain draft. Cryptographic attestation of physical components is cutting-edge.

technical_feasibility.notes: Software SBOM: maturing. Hardware provenance with cryptographic guarantees: early-stage. Requires chip-level identity (ties to HW-01 root-of-trust) plus supply chain tracking infrastructure.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Software side faster (SBOM tooling exists). Hardware side requires vendor cooperation for cryptographic provenance features.

cost.notes: Tracking infrastructure + integration with procurement + ongoing verification. Moderate.

vendor_dependency.notes: Hardware provenance requires vendor embedding cryptographic identity at manufacture time.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Hardware provenance standards and tooling are still emerging
supply_scarcity.notes: Standards bodies working on this but not yet mature.

organizational_readiness.notes: Conceptually understood. Practical implementation depends on ecosystem maturity.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without provenance tracking, a substituted or tampered component cannot be distinguished from a legitimate one by provenance alone. The supply chain becomes a trust-on-first-use system where compromise is undetectable unless caught by physical inspection.

real_world_parallels.description: Pharmaceutical supply chain uses track-and-trace (DSCSA in US) with cryptographic verification to prevent counterfeit drugs. Same concept applied to hardware components.

name: Custom Development of Critical Components
description: Reimplement or custom-develop critical system components when supply chain risk from external sources is unacceptable. Maintain source code, build scripts, and tests internally. Reduces dependency on external vendors for security-critical paths.

current_state.summary: Custom silicon for AI is an established capability at the largest organizations: Google has run production TPUs in its datacenters since 2015-2016, and Amazon (Trainium) and Microsoft (Maia) have since followed. Anthropic confirmed an in-house chip design team in August 2026, framed as part of a multi-chip approach rather than a replacement for vendors. The capability remains limited to a few organizations globally, and most labs rely entirely on external vendors for hardware and much of their software stack.

technical_feasibility.notes: For software: feasible (rewrite critical dependencies internally). For hardware: requires billion-dollar investment and world-class chip design team. Few organizations can do this. For firmware: intermediate difficulty.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Software rewrites: 6-18 months. Custom firmware: 12-24 months. Custom silicon: 36-60 months. Highly variable by component.

cost.notes: Separate per-chip NRE from multi-generation program spend. A leading-edge accelerator tape-out runs roughly $100M-750M all-in depending on node and complexity (mask sets alone $10-20M at 3-5nm), plus $2-5M/year EDA and $5-20M IP licensing. The $1-2B figures quoted for custom silicon programs cover several generations, not one control. Software and firmware rewrites sit at the low end of the range.

vendor_dependency.notes: Reduces vendor dependency (that's the point). Still depends on foundry for manufacturing custom silicon.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Chip designers, security firmware engineers, formal verification experts
supply_scarcity.notes: World-class chip design talent is extremely scarce and expensive.

organizational_readiness.notes: Only viable for the largest AI labs. Creates enormous ongoing maintenance burden. But provides the ultimate supply chain control.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: When using external components, an OC5 adversary can compromise the vendor's design or manufacturing process. Custom development eliminates this vector — the adversary must compromise your internal development instead, which is a fundamentally different (and often harder) attack.

completed_by.why: Building it yourself relocates the supply-chain risk rather than removing it: without a hardware root of trust to anchor what you built and flow-down requirements on your own sub-tier suppliers, the adversary simply targets your build instead of your vendor's.

open_questions.question: Is custom silicon development realistic for any organization other than the very largest?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Most labs cannot implement this block — must rely on commercial vendors with strong inspection/attestation instead

real_world_parallels.description: The US DoD maintains custom ASIC design capability (DMEA) for exactly this reason — when you can't trust commercial supply chains for the most critical components, you build them yourself.
